issues.title: Sharing tick spacing across axes
issues.bodyText:
Sometimes I have a few datasets that need to be plotted each in its subplot.  The datasets don't have the same range (the average values may be somewhat distant), but are still close in their peak-to-peak variation (say within a factor of two).  For example imaging measuring time series of a physical quantity which has slightly different means and standard deviations in multiple experiments.
In this setting, using shared axes is not really suitable (there would be a lot of whitespace left due to different means); on the other hand it is a bit awkward to compare the spreads across the datasets because they are plotted, well, using different scales.  So I'd suggest adding the option to force tick spacing to be the same across multiple axes (so that at least the tick spacing gives an idea of the spread of the data).

issues.title: Inconsistent shape handling of parameter c compared to x/y in scatter()
issues.bodyText:
Bug report
As described in #11663 (review):
Something funny is going on here (I know it was already there before, but still seems worth pointing out): we take x and y of any shapes and flatten them (they just need to have the same size), but c has to match either the shape of x or y, not just the size.
In other words the following "work" (i.e. perform an implicit ravel()):
scatter(np.arange(12).reshape((3, 4)), np.arange(12).reshape((4, 3)), c=np.arange(12).reshape((3, 4)))
scatter(np.arange(12).reshape((3, 4)), np.arange(12).reshape((4, 3)), c=np.arange(12).reshape((4, 3)))

but the following fail:
scatter(np.arange(12).reshape((3, 4)), np.arange(12).reshape((4, 3)), c=np.arange(12).reshape((6, 2)))
# and even
scatter(np.arange(12).reshape((3, 4)), np.arange(12).reshape((4, 3)), c=np.arange(12))

Of course that last one has the best error message (irony intended):

ValueError: 'c' argument has 12 elements, which is not acceptable for use with 'x' with size 12, 'y' with size 12.

comments.bodyText: (I think we should just reject (with deprecation, yada yada) any non-1D input (and yes, that includes (n, 1) and (1, n) input).)
The ravel that we do is a considerable convenience for common use cases such as working with gridded data for ocean or atmospheric fields.

I dunno - it all seems pretty inconsistent to me, like whoever wrote scatter never looked at what plot does, or visce versa, whereas I think they are the same thing.
plt.plot(np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4), np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4))
plt.scatter(np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4), np.arange(12).reshape(3, 4))
are pretty shockingly different.  I'm fine w/ them being different, but I'm somewhat against scatter just flattening the array without comment.  I think I'd go with @anntzer's proposal so the difference is explicit.  Its not like scatter(X.flat, Y.flat) is so hard...
If they were the same thing we wouldn't need both.  They are intentionally different.  Where their purposes overlap, we recommend using plot.

Still we should aim at consistent API where possible.
I don't see an argument for different handling of mutl-dimensional data

of parameter  c vs parameters x, y  in scatter()
of parameters x, y in scatter()  vs plot()

In scatter, c can be an array of color specs, including rgb or rgba, which means, for example, that if x and y are 1D, c can be 2D, with its first dimension matching the lengths of x and y.  Or it could be a single color spec, which could be a string, a scalar, or an rgb or rgba sequence. Therefore, we must handle c a bit differently than 'x' and 'y'.
x and y are handled differently in scatter() vs plot() because these two functions overlap, but are still fundamentally different.  plot plots one or more lines (whether using an actual line for each, or a set of identical points for each, or both).  scatter just plots a set--a single set--of points, but it allows the size and color of each point to be specified individually.

I disagree.  Relative to #13959, I don't think that removing the flattening makes anything substantially simpler or more consistent.  It would break existing code for no gain that I can see, and would require adding shape checking in place of size checking.  Really, what is the big gain here, to motivate a considerable break in backward compatibility?  I just don't see it.  (And removing the flattening does not remove differences between x, y, and c handling.)
#13959 is making things more consistent in scatter.  What's wrong with it?
If we were starting from scratch, and if we took the point of view that we should keep the API as simple as possible and leave it to the user to make their data fit that API, then it might make sense to require that x and y be 1-D, since logically and in practice they are within the function.  But we are not starting from scratch--we have a long history and an admittedly imperfect heritage--and our general practice in the high-level API has been to try to make things easy for the end user, to make things work if they logically can.  In fact we have been adding such things, not removing them: witness the support for pandas-like data structures.

Reconsidered. Actually, it can be reasonable to support 2D arrays as scatter input. For some kinds of scatter plots x and y can be semantically the same type e.g. positions in a plane (as opposed to y = f(x)). And if these are aligned on a regular grid, a 2D shape may be the natural form of the input data.

issues.title: Remove()ing a shared axes prevents the remaining axes from using unit-provided formatters
issues.bodyText:
Consider
from pylab import *
from datetime import date

fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, sharex=True)
axs[1].remove()
axs[0].plot([date(2000, 1, 1), date(2000, 2, 1)], [0, 1])
plt.show()

One gets

i.e. the call to axs[1].remove() prevented the axs[0] from acquiring the correct tick formatter and locator.
Interestingly, using fig.delaxes(axs[1]) doesn't exhibit the same bug.
Looks like the problem comes from
    def _remove_ax(self, ax):
        def _reset_loc_form(axis):
            axis.set_major_formatter(axis.get_major_formatter())
            axis.set_major_locator(axis.get_major_locator())
            axis.set_minor_formatter(axis.get_minor_formatter())
            axis.set_minor_locator(axis.get_minor_locator())

        def _break_share_link(ax, grouper):
            siblings = grouper.get_siblings(ax)
            if len(siblings) > 1:
                grouper.remove(ax)
                for last_ax in siblings:
                    if ax is not last_ax:
                        return last_ax
            return None

        self.delaxes(ax)
        last_ax = _break_share_link(ax, ax._shared_y_axes)
        if last_ax is not None:
            _reset_loc_form(last_ax.yaxis)

        last_ax = _break_share_link(ax, ax._shared_x_axes)
        if last_ax is not None:
            _reset_loc_form(last_ax.xaxis)

where the call to set_major_formatter (etc.), which basically call formatter.set_axis(axis) (to update the axis seen by the formatter) also make Matplotlib believe that we had a user-provided formatter (isDefault_majloc = False, etc.) which should not be overridden by the unit framework.

issues.title: constrained_layout support for figure.legend
issues.bodyText: Just a feature request to have constrained_layout support figure.legend

comments.bodyText:
What behaviour would you expect?
If you want the legend to steal space on the figure from the axes, then call axes.legend with the correct handles and it will make room.
Yes. Here's an example from seaborn. I would expect this to be the result of figure.legend(handles, labels, loc='right')

How would constrained layout know which subplots to steal space from for the legend?   A figure legend doesn’t belong to any axes, so there is no natural way to do what you are asking.
Again if you attach the legend to one of the rightmost axes, it will do what you want.

How would constrained layout know which subplots to steal space from for the legend?

Do what colorbar does? colorbar does have an ax argument though... hmmm.
Here's an example. I'd like the constrained_layout version of this:
f, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, sharex=True, sharey=True, constrained_layout=False)
h = list()
for aa in ax.flat:
    h.append(aa.plot(np.random.randn(5), np.random.randn(5), '*')[0])
    h.append(aa.plot(np.random.randn(5), np.random.randn(5), '*')[0])

hleg = f.legend(handles=h[-2:], labels=['a', 'b'],
                loc='center right')

Here's my attempt at a constrained_layout version using ax.legend. Is there a way to do this without the space between the two rows of subplots?
f, ax = plt.subplots(2, 2, sharex=True, sharey=True, constrained_layout=True)
h = list()
for aa in ax.flat:
    h.append(aa.plot(np.random.randn(5), np.random.randn(5), '*')[0])
    h.append(aa.plot(np.random.randn(5), np.random.randn(5), '*')[0])

hleg = ax[1, 1].legend(handles=h[-2:], labels=['a', 'b'],
                       loc='center right',
                       bbox_to_anchor=(1.2, 1.2))

What is happening above is ax[1, 1] is saying it is bigger than the other axes, and makes space for itself in the layout.  To avoid this, don't anchor it above the top of the axes.  Yes, your legend will not be vertically centred.
We could come up with an API to automatically insert anchored boxes and steal space from the other elements in a gridspec (the container of your four subplots).  We do that now for suptitle (sort of) and, as you say, colorbar.  So the question is how to pass that info down to fig.legend.  I suppose we could add an axs kwarg.

Thought about this some more, and its quite a hard problem.
figure.legend allows more than one legend. Conversely, figure.suptitle only has one suptitle, so layout is easy.  figure.colorbar has a well-understood set of conventions for where colorbars go, but legends have been more free-form, with placement being arbitrary, and anchored using bbox_to_anchor.
Is it feasible to only add support for certain legend configurations in a first step? E.g. don‘t handle legends with bbox_to_anchor and/or certain loc values.
I was going to say the same. The loc values should be well constrained and a good first step. Throw a warning and disable constrained_layout if bbox_to_anchor is set?

Hmmmm.  Not a fan of that.  Seems mysterious and a documentation PITA
I was leaning towards a new method, ideally  attached to gridspec. That’s easier from the point of view of being able to specify a new API.
I think conceptually this is easy enough to implement in constrained_layout.  But I’m not sure about implementing without constrained_layout.  Legends are packable boxes and hence hard to predict their size a priori.  For instance they can be arbitrarily wide or high.
I’d propose writing a separate method for now and then figure.legend could call that given the right conditions.

I’d propose writing a separate method for now and then figure.legend could call that given the right conditions.

Sounds like a reasonable approach. Though, I'm not quite involved in this stuff, and therefore I'm not a good judge. Withdrawing from the discussion for now.

I have a proof of concept that works great for this.  Up for ideas about how to specify locations and whether the arrangement with the rest of the gridspec is horizontal or vertical.   The typical location “northeast” or “southeast” is ambiguous because it doesn’t specify if the gridspec’s Axes give way vertically or horizontally.  We’d could either have another kwarg, or let the location=“verticalnortheast” to specify vertical arrangement instead of horizontal (which I think would be the default for all locations except for “north” and “south”)...
Suggestions welcome.   For now, I think I’ll go w/ implementing horizontal arrangement, and just not support “north” or “south” (I.e. “northeast” will arrange horizontally, with the legend in the upper right corner).
Using an extra kwarg arrange=vertical or arrange=horizontal seems less clunky than verticalnortheast

issues.title: `ax.set_prop_cycle` does not allow 'CN' colors
issues.bodyText:
Hi matplotlib developers,
I was surprised to discover that the cycler validation does not allow colors specified with 'CN' syntax.
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from cycler import cycler

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.set_prop_cycle(cycler(color=['C1', 'C0'])) # raises ValueError
# ax.set_prop_cycle(cycler(color=['tab:orange', 'tab:blue'])) # works fine
ax.plot(np.arange(9))
ax.plot(-np.arange(9))
plt.show()
If matplotlib can differentiate between {'C0', 'C1', 'C2', 'C3', 'C4', 'C5', 'C6', 'C7', 'C8', 'C9'} colors and {'b', 'g', 'r', 'c', 'm', 'y', 'k', 'w'} colors (case insensitive) anywhere else that a color is specified, then it seems to me that the cycler should be able to handle this as well. Thanks.
Tested with matplotlib 3.0.3 and python 3.7.3 (Anaconda) on Windows 10.

comments.bodyText: That cannot be done reliably. 'CN' indexes into the default property cycle at execution time, which then just might be the cycler you created. Therefore cyclers themselves do not accept 'CN'.

@timhoffm Thanks for the comment, but I don't fully understand. Are you saying it is a recursion issue? Why can't the cycler evaluate its input arguments at instantiation using the "currently defined" cycler, then use those values to create the "new" cycler?

Cyclers don't do anything at instantiation time. Actually, it's not even the cycler that resolves the color. The color is resolved in the respective plotting function when it's called. issues.title: Add easily comparable version info to toplevel
issues.bodyText:
Problem
Currently matplotlib only exposes __version__.  For quick version checks, exposing either a version_info tuple (which can be compared with other tuples) or a LooseVersion instance (which can be properly compared with other strings) would be a small usability improvement.
(In practice I guess boring string comparisons will work just fine until we hit mpl 3.10 or 4.10 which is unlikely to happen soon, but that feels quite dirty :))

Proposed Solution
I guess I slightly prefer LooseVersion, but exposing just a version_info tuple is much more common in other packages (and perhaps simpler to understand).  The hardest(?) part is probably just bikeshedding this point :-)

Additional context and prior art
version_info is a pretty common thing (citation needed).

comments.bodyText:
It seems that __version_info__ is the way to go.
Prior art


There's no official specification for version tuples. PEP 396 - Module Version Numbers only defines the string __version__.


Many projects don't bother with version tuples.


When they do, __version_info__ seems to be a common thing:

Stackoverflow discussion
PySide2 uses it.



Python itself has the string sys.version and the (named)tuple sys.version_info. In analogy to that __version_info__ next to __version__ makes sense for packages.

issues.title: Should zero-sized Rectangles be taken into account for autoscaling purposes?
issues.bodyText:
Currently, Rectangles with zero-width and zero-height are ignored for autoscaling purposes, but not other zero-sized patches:
from matplotlib import patches, pyplot as plt

ax = plt.figure().add_subplot()
ax.add_patch(patches.Rectangle((-5, -5), 0, 0))  # zero-sized at (-5, -5)
ax.add_patch(patches.Circle((5, 5), 0))  # zero-radius at (5, 5)
ax.relim()
ax.autoscale_view()
plt.show()
results in axes autoscaled around (5, 5) (so they include the circle, but not the rectangle).  I would argue that Rectangles should never be ignored, even if they have zero-width and zero-height, both for consistency with other patches, and because such Rectangles are likely not drawn with no reason.
This behavior (implemented in Axes._update_patch_limits) was introduced in f24d06c to support log-scaled histograms with empty bins, but is not necessary anymore as hist autoscaling was fully reworked in #14581, making this behavior unnecessary (the check in _update_patch_limits can be deleted with no bad effects); perhaps it was even already unnecessary before though.
Also, note that #2942 already weakened the original patch by going from ignoring Rectangles with zero width OR height to only ignoring Rectangles with zero width and height.

Problem
For SVG output I believe the only way to suppress metadata output is to manually set all relevant fields (Date, Creator, Format, Type, etc.) to None.  There should be an easier way to do so, either by passing metadata={} or by passing metadata=None.  Hopefully this can be made consistent with the other backends too...

Support either metadata={} or metadata=None to mean "suppress all metadata".

comments.bodyText:
The following calls to FigureCanvasSVG.print_svg() are currently identical
print_svg(filename)
print_svg(filename, metadata=None)
print_svg(filename, metadata={})

and they use the predefined defaults (https://matplotlib.org/3.3.3/api/backend_svg_api.html?matplotlib.backends.backend_svg.FigureCanvasSVG.print_svg)

Values have been predefined for 'Creator', 'Date', 'Format', and 'Type'. They can be removed by setting them to None.

This means that the proposed solution is an API change.
I rule out the proposal metadata={}: {Creator='me'} will lead to all defaults being used and, it'd be a discontinuity if removing the Author would remove all other defaults.
metadata=None is a bit tricky because it's used as default value in the internal _print_svg and in RendererSVG and we'd have to work around that.

metadata=None, and changing the default sentinel. - This is an API change again, but low-impact.
metadata=None, and expanding that in print_svg() to {'Creator'=None, 'Date'=None, ..., }. - A bit too hacky for my taste.
metadata='none' - 'none' is a common pattern in Matplotlib for visuals, but not in other contexts.

I slightly tend towards the first solution.
We could consider adding a _NoValue singleton that serves as default and is distinguished from None.  (See e.g. np._NoValue for prior art.)

This came in #20161.  @timhoffm any ideas here?
(I don't know if this should block 3.4.3, but if it can be fixed it likely should be).

The relevant bit of the change is here. Clearing the tick keyword dictionaries drops the settings for which sides the ticks should be visible.

issues.title: [ENH]: Auto-detect location/orientation of colorbar with user-set cax based on cax position relative to mappable axes
issues.bodyText:
Problem
In the case of calling colorbar(mappable, cax) where cax is explicitly constructed by the user and mappable also has an .axes set (typically, mappable is an actual artist already on the figure), colorbar() could auto-determine the values of the location and orientation kwargs (currently always defaulting to "right"/"vertical") based on the relative position of cax relative to mappable.axes (and perhaps also the aspect ratio of cax):

Define the region "above" of mappable.axes as the region just above it (y >= mappable.ymax, mappable.xmin <= x <= mappable.xmax), and likewise the regions "below", "to the left", and "to the right".  There are also corners ("top left", etc.).  Determine which regions of mappable.axes are overlapped by cax.
If cax only overlaps the "above" region and possibly the "top left" and "top right" corners or mappable.axes itself, set location to "top".  Ditto for the three other sides.

The other cases are a bit pathological (except for the corner case (*), they imply that cax overlaps mappable.axes, which is probably extremely rare in practice), but listed for completeness.

If cax overlaps both "above" and "left" (and thus "top left" and mappable.axes itself too), or only (*)) the "top left" corner, set location to "top" or "left" depending on whether the axes is wider or taller (breaking ties in favor of vertical, which is the default colorbar orientation).  Ditto for other corners.

Hi @jklymak! While I agree that polar is a radius/angle coordinate system, the quiver documentation for xy says "'xy': "Arrow direction in data coordinates, i.e. the arrows point from (x, y) to (x+u, y+v). Use this e.g. for plotting a gradient field." It is not at all clear that this means that u and v should be radius and angle.
If this is the case, this should be outlined specifically in the documentation, as it's highly unclear and I've spent quite a lot of time struggling to decipher how this should work.

And actually, I'd strongly argue that angles="xy" shouldn't work like this, as the intention of the angles="xy" argument is clearly that you can plot data using quiver without needing to calculate every angle beforehand, and if passing angles="xy" basically means you have to manually calculate both the radius and angle of each vector, it means that it's always easier to pass the lat of the vector to U, the lon to V and the angle to angles, which seems weird. (In that case, I'd argue that angles="xy" should throw an error or at least a warning, since it is so counterintuitive.)

Quiver doesn't know what projection is being used.  It draws arrows from (x, y) to (x+u, y+v).  Despite the bad name for u and v, its should be clear that they need to be in the same units as x and y.  Anything else is ambiguous.

(In that case, I'd argue that angles="xy" should throw an error or at least a warning, since it is so counterintuitive.)

and if passing angles="xy" basically means you have to manually calculate both the radius and angle of each vector,

Just to be clear, quiver is largely designed with Cartesian axes in mind.  Indeed parameters like scale make it clear it was largely designed with isotropic Cartesian axes in mind. Do we want to say anything about how we expect our event timers to behave with regard to when they fire? Should a timer be ticking continuously and firing when requested regardless of other tasks occurring (maybe in a separate thread), or should the timers fire at (time in callback + interval)?
Following up with some results about what the various backends currently do for callbacks that last longer than the timers with the following test script that will either print ~1/second or every 2-seconds.

    print(time.ctime())
    time.sleep(1)

timer = fig.canvas.new_timer(interval=1000)
timer.add_callback(on_timer)
timer.start()
fig.canvas.start_event_loop(10)

qtagg: 1-second
gtk4agg: 1-second

Originally posted by @greglucas in #29023 (comment)

comments.bodyText: You can imagine either behaviour is desired.  Certainly it should be the same between backends!

Timers are internally mostly (only?) used for animations, and if I request a 1fps animation I don't care how much time matplotlib takes to render the canvas, so I would think that requesting a 1s interval should lead to a trigger every second (to the extent where this is possible), even if the callback takes 950ms to execute?
I'm also in favor of doing our best to hit the requested trigger rate (independent if we spend that time doing stuff or letting the event loop twiddle its thumbs).
What do you intend to happen when the callback takes longer than the timer duration?
Then we just run as fast as possible?
But does the callback overlap or only run once after?
I think they all run in the same thread, so they can't overlap, can they?

Sorry, not overlap, but bunch up. Say you have a 1-second timer, and your callback takes a fraction of second, except one time it's doing file I/O or something, and takes 5 seconds. Do you get one call at the sixth second after that one started, or 5? Your "as fast as possible" could be interpreted either way.
Now, I'm pretty sure all our toolkits say that you will get 1, but if we start fiddling with things, then we should codify that that's what we expect as well.
Good question.  I would probably go for option 1, but it's not something I have properly thought about.

Currently all timers are added to the main thread of the respective toolkit, and all work is also scheduled on that thread (unless the callback spawns a separate thread itself). This means that the timer doesn't fire during the long callback, so there is not a buildup of events.
An example script to demonstrate all of this and the current inconsistencies between backends is here:

    else:
        time.sleep(0.1)
    x += 1

timer = fig.canvas.new_timer(interval=200)
timer.add_callback(on_timer)
timer.start()
fig.canvas.start_event_loop(2)

issues.title: [ENH]: Built-in crosshair tool through gui-native crosshair cursor
issues.bodyText:
Problem
Our naive approaches to crosshair cursors https://matplotlib.org/devdocs/gallery/widgets/cursor.html have the disadvantage that the crosshair is drawn on the figure. This means an expensive redraw of the the figure for every cursor position change and results in a laggy behavior.
Proposed solution
We could grow an API on Canvas to draw a crosshair with GUI native lines. That should be relatively easy. We only need the size of the Axes-under-cursor in figure coordinates to determine the length of the crosshair.
The goal would be to add a crosshair tool in addtion to Pan and Zoom.
This tool should be much easier to use than a Cursor widget and much more efficient.

Hi @timhoffm,
I spent some time going through this issue and the related discussions about overlays and the crosshair cursor. To understand the problem better, I also explored parts of Matplotlib’s rendering pipeline to see where the performance limitations might arise.
From what I understand, the main challenge is that interactive elements like crosshair cursors are currently implemented as Artists that participate in the normal draw pipeline. Because of this, every cursor movement triggers the entire rendering process (FigureCanvasBase.draw -Figure.draw-Axes.draw-Artists).
For elements that update very frequently, such as cursors or selectors, this can become quite expensive and can introduce noticeable lag.
The overlay concept seems intended to address this by separating the rendering of the static figure from rapidly changing interactive elements.
Based on the discussion, it looks like there are two possible directions for implementing this.
(a) GUI-native overlay primitives:
One option would be for each backend to draw overlay primitives directly using the GUI toolkit’s native drawing capabilities.
Advantages:
1)Very fast updates since this bypasses Matplotlib’s main rendering pipeline.
2)The figure itself does not need to be redrawn.
Limitations:
1)Each backend would need its own implementation.
2)Maintaining consistent behavior across backends could become challenging.
3)It may also reduce flexibility if overlays need deeper integration with Matplotlib objects.
(b) A Matplotlib-managed overlay layer:
Another approach would be to introduce a dedicated overlay layer within Matplotlib itself. This layer would be rendered separately from the main figure image and composited on top of it.
Advantages:
1)More backend-independent design.
2)Could potentially evolve into a more general layered rendering architecture.
3)Might unify or simplify existing mechanisms such as widget blitting or animation updates.
Challenges:
1)It would require careful design around layer coordination (coordinate systems, event handling, and draw order).
2)Overlay updates would still need to remain lightweight to ensure smooth interaction.
The idea of expanding this into a general layered drawing system seems particularly interesting. For instance, we could imagine a structure like:

a static background layer for expensive plots
a dynamic overlay layer for elements like crosshairs, selectors, or cursors
a foreground layer for annotations or temporary UI elements

With this setup, only the dynamic layer would need to be updated during interaction, while the other layers remain unchanged. This might also help simplify the current blitting logic used by widgets and animations.
As a next step, I plan to continue looking into the backend canvas implementations and the draw pipeline to understand where a layered system like this could integrate most cleanly.
One question I had while thinking about the architecture:
Would it make more sense for the overlay system to live at the canvas level (inside FigureCanvasBase), acting as a composition layer, or closer to the Figure level, but rendered separately from the main draw pass?
Thanks for the guidance -this is a really interesting architectural topic, and I’m looking forward to exploring it further.

Hi @timhoffm,
Following up on the discussion about the two approaches, I was curious about the actual performance hit of Approach (b)—specifically the alpha compositing overhead if Matplotlib tries to manage the overlay layer itself.
I wrote a quick script to benchmark full-canvas blending (1920x1080) in pure NumPy versus just offloading a transparent QWidget to the OS window manager using PyQt6.
The difference is pretty massive. Doing the array blending in NumPy takes about ~31.7 ms per frame on my machine (roughly 31 FPS), which would definitely feel laggy for a fast-moving crosshair. On the other hand, the Qt hardware compositing is basically free, taking only ~0.035 ms per frame.
It seems like a pure Matplotlib-managed layer (Approach B) is going to be too slow out of the box unless we restrict the pixel blending to a small bounding box around the cursor. But wouldn't that just reintroduce the same region-tracking headaches we already deal with using blitting?
Given this performance gap, do you think Approach (a) (GUI-native primitives) is the more realistic path forward, even though it means writing separate implementations for each backend?

From the results, it seems that doing a full-canvas alpha blending step in Python/NumPy could introduce noticeable latency, especially for larger figures. That makes it clear why GUI-native rendering could provide much smoother updates for interactive overlays.
At the same time, I was wondering if a hybrid approach might work.
For example, Matplotlib could provide a general overlay API at the canvas level, while each backend implements the rendering using the most efficient approach available.
In that case:
GUI backends such as Qt, GTK, or Tk could render overlays using native drawing primitives or hardware compositing.
Non-interactive backends could fall back to a lightweight Matplotlib-based implementation if needed.
This might allow Matplotlib to keep a consistent interface while still benefiting from hardware-accelerated rendering in GUI environments.
Right now I’m continuing to explore the backend implementations (starting with the Qt backend) to better understand how the draw pipeline and event handling interact inside FigureCanvasBase. I also plan to look more closely at how blitting and partial redraws are currently used by widgets and animations, to see if similar region-based updates could help keep overlay updates lightweight.

Separation & Invalidation: Artists are assigned to layers (e.g., Layer 0: Static plot, Layer 1: Interactive crosshair). When a widget updates its coordinates, it naturally triggers self.invalidate().

The Math: The LayerManager intercepts this and calculates the exact changed region using Bbox.union([old_bbox, new_bbox]).

Smart Compositing: During the draw pass, the manager skips rendering for valid layers (reusing their cached pixel buffers). It commands the backend to re-render the dirty layers only inside that specific Bbox union, and then alpha-composites just that tiny fraction of the screen.
